extracted.intended_audience: orators, poets, writers, and students of rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing elevated, persuasive, and passionate speech or prose (the ‘sublime’) via imagery, figures, diction, rhythm, and rhetorical devices. Emphasises when devices enhance or damage sublimity and how to deploy them for maximal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality and truth in oratorical imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: In oratory the best feature of imagery is always its reality and truth; poetical/fabulous extravagances tend to transcend credibility and give an alien air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid poetical impossibilities and extravagant fancies that belong to tragic/mad characters (e.g., seeing Furies) — such digressions sound strange in oratory. Use imagery that feels real to maintain persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery as vehicle of vehemence and persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery, when combined with argumentative passages, infuses vehemence and passion and can not only persuade but make the hearer its slave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use startling, dazzling images to draw attention away from bare demonstration and to conceal the argument within vivid conception (example: Demosthenes' prison-house/flight illustration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of apostrophe/oath
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath or apostrophe can deify ancestors and transform a reasoned argument into transcendent sublimity and passion when placed and framed properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity of oath depends on place, manner, circumstances, and motive — choose the object you swear by carefully (Demosthenes' oath by champions of Greece vs. Eupolis' less apt example). Use sobriety and precise word choice to avoid incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of rhetorical figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures are most effective when their artifices escape attention; if the audience perceives a crafty figure it raises suspicion and may provoke resentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially before judges, despots, or superior persons do not make the figure obvious. Hide the craft by associating figures with overwhelming sublimity or passion so artifice fades from view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity and passion as antidote to suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity and passionate grandeur throw rhetorical artifices into the shade, preventing future suspicion of craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intense light/overwhelming grandeur (figurative 'excess of light') so the audience perceives the sublime first and not the figure; let passion naturalize the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical questions and simulated dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions and interrogations (and asking-and-answering oneself) visualize issues and make speech more effective and convincing by simulating spontaneous passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ question-and-answer to meet objections and to create the appearance of unpremeditated outburst; rapid play of questions increases excitement and believability (Demosthenes examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of conjunctions / broken sentences for agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Words detached from one another, with omission of conjunctions or broken sentences, produce an impression of agitation and impetuosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clipped, hurried phrasing to mimic action or excitement (Homeric example). Avoid smoothing with conjunctions when you want to convey rapid motion or fury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of multiple figures for cumulative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two or three figures (e.g., broken sentences, repetition, vivid description) can mingle in partnership to produce strength, persuasiveness, and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interweave devices (repetition + broken sentences + vivid detail) to mimic the effect of a physical assault: 'strike on strike.' Vary continually to maintain momentum and avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid smoothing passion with connecting particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding copulatives and connecting particles (making an orderly version) blunts the rugged impetuosity of passion and causes the passage to lose its fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not transcribe passionate, broken passages into neat, orderly prose; restraining connectors act like binding limbs of runners — they restrict rapid motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion/transposition to convey vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: Departures from the natural order of expressions or ideas (inversions) bear the stamp of vehement emotion and make speech seem unpremeditated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postpone subjects, state reasons before exhortation, or rearrange clauses to create urgency and spontaneity (Dionysius, Thucydides, Demosthenes examples). Use boldly but with awareness of listener comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long inversions to create suspense and shared peril
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy transpositions that disjoin elements normally united leave thoughts in suspense and compel the hearer into anxious sympathy, producing a powerful effect when resolved at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve long, hazardous inversions for moments of high risk; they produce a dramatic payoff when the awaited conclusion arrives (use sparingly as they are bold and perilous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation, variation, and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of accumulation, variation, and climax are prime rhetorical weapons that contribute to elegance, sublimity, and passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graded lists, repetitions with variation, and rising sequences to build force; vary cases, tenses, persons, numbers, genders to diversify exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of number (plural vs singular) for rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the plural where a singular might suffice amplifies sense of multitude; compressing plurals into a singular can give the feeling of unified body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pluralization to pluralize misfortunes or emphasize multitude; compress to singular to convey unity. Do so only where the subject admits amplification, redundancy, exaggeration, or passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical present (presenting past as immediate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing past events as if taking place now converts narration into actuality and heightens immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the historical present to bring the listener 'into the scene' (characteristic of Thucydides, used by Xenophon). Apply where vividness trumps strict chronological narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange of persons and direct address
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting persons and addressing the hearer or a single individual places the hearer on the scene and increases active participation and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak as 'you' or to a specific individual to quicken response and make the audience feel personally concerned. Use direct address to keep the hearer alert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden conversion of narrator into character
rubrics_metrics.description: Abruptly attributing narrated speech to a character (narrator suddenly becomes that person) produces an outburst of passion and dramatic immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this device at sharp crises where pause is not permitted; avoid prefatory 'he said' tags—let the abrupt transition convey fury or determination (Homer, Demosthenes examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis as harmonising accompaniment
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumlocution (periphrasis) can harmonise with simple expression and add melodic rhythm and beauty, enriching the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasteful, tempered periphrasis to add melodic harmony (Plato's Funeral Oration example). Ensure it is not inflated or dissonant; keep it well-tempered and apt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard of periphrasis (avoid empty amplitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis is hazardous: if handled without discrimination it becomes empty, swollen, and odorous of empty talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overblown circumlocution (critique of Plato's Laws). Be wary of prolix euphemism that masks triviality or leads to ridiculous phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of striking, appropriate words
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of proper, striking words attracts and enthralls the hearer; such diction is the leading ambition of orators and writers and conveys grandeur, dignity, force, and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction to subject — stately language should not be used for petty affairs. Use expressive, vivid words (including homely or colloquial phrasing when more telling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of homely/plain expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Homely or familiar expressions can be sometimes more telling than elegant language because they are immediately understood and convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't reject colloquial phrasing when it conveys character or vividness ('stomaching things' example). Avoid vulgarity only insofar as it detracts from expressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate number and boldness of metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional counsel limits metaphors to one or at most three in a passage, but when passions surge many metaphors are permissible and their number is justified by fervour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use many metaphors only when passion or descriptive frenzy carries the audience; soften bold metaphors with qualifiers ('as if', 'as it were') when necessary to mitigate audacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphors best in impassioned/descriptive passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors and tropes thrive in impassioned and descriptive writing; they are natural to such passages but prone to excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metaphors heavily for vivid description (Plato, Xenophon examples), but beware of frenzy that makes metaphors harsh or inflated; moderate or trim where excess undermines clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for faults with higher excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: Lofty genius and great elevation of spirit may include oversights and faults; higher excellences of quality should be preferred to moderate but flawless success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging writings, favour works with extraordinary elevation or force even if they contain occasional slips (Homer preferred to more faultless but lesser writers). Be aware that superior excellences may come with attendant errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over quantity of merits in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater number of smaller excellences does not necessarily outrank fewer but higher-quality excellences; superiority in quality can trump numerical variety of merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate variety of acceptable traits with ultimate greatness (Hyperides vs Demosthenes example); assess the height and depth of singular excellences rather than tallying features.
